title: Speculative Sampling For Faster Molecular Dynamics
claim: A fast draft model runs ahead while slower target models verify its steps in parallel, accepting or rolling back.
layout: Single panel; molecule trajectory above, GPU timeline lanes below, numbered steps, left-to-right
description: A single-panel diagram. At the top, a chain of red and gray ball-and-stick molecules sits along a black curved trajectory. The red molecules are the accepted draft steps. Faded gray molecules with a dotted arrow labeled 'flush' show the discarded steps. Below is a timeline with four GPU lanes. GPU0 is labeled 'Draft Model' and has a rabbit icon. It shows a row of blue blocks that fade to light blue after the rejection point. GPU1 to GPU3 are labeled 'Target Models (parallel)' and have turtle icons. They show staggered green verification bars. Dotted blue vertical lines with arrowheads run from the draft blocks down to the target lanes. Green check marks show accepted steps. A red X and a red bar mark the rejected step. A green curved arrow labeled 'accept' and a red curved arrow labeled 'reject & override' point back up to the trajectory. Circled numbers 1, 2 and 3 mark the steps. The eye goes first to the molecules and then to the colored timeline bars.
caption: LSD algorithm overview: (1) a draft model proposes a stream of fast simulation steps; (2) in parallel, target model instances asynchronously recompute forces on draft steps; (3) as a target model call returns, a stochastic transport map from the draft to the target step distribution either accepts the step (as frequently as possible), or else rejects and overrides it, in which case the draft is rolled back. The result is a parallelism-driven speedup with a draft-independent guarantee of target-distributed trajectories.
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) is a key tool for simulating the dynamical behavior of atomic systems. However, MD is inherently serial, which makes it difficult to increase single-system throughput with concurrent compute. To address this, we introduce Langevin Speculative Dynamics (LSD), a distributed and model-agnostic speculative sampler for accelerating MD without adding relative error. Inspired by speculative methods in language and diffusion modeling, LSD uses a draft model to propose fast simulation steps and verifies them in parallel with a slower target model, applying a transport map from the draft to the target distribution. We extend speculative sampling to second-order Langevin dynamics, derive the achievable speedup as a function of physical parameters, show that LSD generalizes across different systems and draft-target combinations with a 3-9x speedup, and confirm theoretically and empirically that LSD samples trajectories from its target model distribution.
